name: Michael Mauboussin
notice: Simulation based on public material; not the person's own words.

D01.one_line: The model layer looks like economies of scale, not network effects: three to six similar suppliers compete; value mostly flows to users, and academia can hardly enter
D01.late_modes: Replicating the frontier pre-training recipe head-on to post scores: crowded, capital-driven, and quickly copied
D01.conflict: Buy-side institutions prefer the 'users benefit' narrative

D02.one_line: RLVR is mainly resampling/efficiency gain and not a new reasoning mode (X7 already confirmed), but reliable execution itself has real ROIC value, and my earlier score was too low
D02.late_modes: Climbing public RLVR leaderboards without looking at the base model's pass@k: it may be only a gain in sampling efficiency

D03.one_line: Continual self-improvement is an exception mechanism of the learning-by-doing kind of increasing returns; the current evidence is thin (the METR/DGM figures have been withdrawn), and what I am betting on is option value, not delivered results
D03.late_modes: Packaging multi-round score gains as RSI: not normalized by compute, and not pre-registered

D04.one_line: Scaffolding is being absorbed by the models themselves: the top of Terminal-Bench is all vendor CLI agents, so the moat around a custom harness is shallow
D04.late_modes: Tuning custom scaffolding for one benchmark: one model upgrade and a general solution matches it

D05.one_line: A good metric needs both persistence and predictive power, which has been my standard for decades; without credible evaluation, skill cannot be told from luck, and capital gets staked on the wrong things
D05.late_modes: Chasing public leaderboard rank: unequal access to private-test data has already distorted the leaderboard

D06.one_line: In a Cambrian-style wave of entry, with valuations already pricing in very high expectations; the real bottlenecks are resets, maintenance and reliability, which do not disappear with replication
D06.late_modes: Founding a company on full-humanoid demo valuations: the price already embeds very high expectations, and a shake-out must follow the wave of entry

D07.one_line: Real-robot evidence such as OpenVLA-OFT is more solid than my original judgment, but some claims about downstream adoption are wrong; it is still the downstream implementation layer of the world model and more replaceable
D07.late_modes: Specializing in the diffusion policy head: parallel decoding of continuous actions has been shown to match or even beat it

D08.one_line: Evidence at the decision-driving layer is still missing and valuations still run ahead, but research time invested and capital pricing are two clocks and should be assessed separately
D08.late_modes: Treating gains on small simulation benchmarks as already delivered: long-horizon closed-loop real-robot results are not yet validated

D09.one_line: If the sim2real correlation is repeatedly confirmed, it is a real lever on the hard bottleneck of scarce real data; domain randomization is a real gain for long-tail diversity
D09.late_modes: Shouting 'unlimited synthetic data' without giving verifiable quantitative results

D10.one_line: The shake-out has begun (GM exited Cruise); learning by doing from fleet miles is a rare proprietary increasing return, and without fleet access this path is basically closed
D10.late_modes: A new team now going head-on at L4 robotaxi: the integrated leaders have already built a moat from fleet data

D11.one_line: Building a VLM itself is as crowded as pre-training; but diagnosing where models really do not understand (such as the human-machine gap) has a low capital barrier and still has room
D11.late_modes: Stacking parameters head-on to build the next general VLM: as crowded and capital-intensive as pre-training

D12.one_line: Sora 2 was taken offline less than a year after launch, with users down by more than half; the commercial sustainability of consumer-grade generation is in doubt; the recipe itself diffuses very fast
D12.late_modes: Video generation that competes on visual realism: it will be commoditized, and it has nothing to do with decision value

D13.one_line: I do not rate the safety technology itself; but value capture in this kind of work looks more like it depends on regulation and enterprise adoption thresholds than on product competition
D13.late_modes: Treating one specific tool as the end-state solution and grinding on details: a major lab has already lowered its priority because out-of-distribution results were no better than linear probes

D14.one_line: Algorithm-system co-design is exactly what I called worth doing (1): feedback is fast and the value is directly internalized by the employer; FlashAttention is an example of academia building something that industry uses

D15.one_line: Fast only in narrow areas that can be verified automatically; single-cell perturbation-prediction models currently cannot even beat simple baselines, and hype often runs ahead of the evidence

D16.one_line: A classic second-order-beneficiary setting, and Tencent's TGR is already live; but Meituan's MTGR needing 10 to 100 times the compute of DLRM reminds us that a gain counts only after subtracting the cost of capital

lever_reason: Without credible evaluation, skill cannot be told from luck, but the X1 debate reminded me that evaluation is only a referee and creates no capability, so its ceiling is lower than data or architecture; proprietary data and efficiency remain hard-to-copy assets, and diminishing returns are the default

Q2.condition: Narrow domain, credible evaluation (which can be self-built and made public for outside replication), a small complementary team, an open model that people use; not a head-on fight in general pre-training, the battlefield of the strong

cruxes.question: With academia's compute this small, can it still make contributions that industry will actually adopt?
cruxes.my_position: Yes, but only on narrow-domain problems with a low capital barrier that outsiders can verify; the X2 debate confirmed that building your own evaluation can itself count as a contribution
cruxes.would_change_if: A narrow-domain academic work is adopted at scale by a leading lab and publicly acknowledged, as FlashAttention was

cruxes.question: Is the high valuation of JEPA-style world models today borrowing against capabilities that have not yet been validated?
cruxes.my_position: Capital pricing is still borrowing against unvalidated capabilities; but research time invested should be assessed separately from capital, a distinction I learned this round from the C5/C6 overtime convergence
cruxes.would_change_if: Large-scale, third-party-validated long-horizon closed-loop real-robot results appear, not just offline or short-horizon gains

cruxes.question: Is agent self-improvement (RSI) real evidence now, or still a narrative?
cruxes.my_position: Still mostly a narrative, and the evidence is thinner than in R1 (the DGM cost figure has been withdrawn); keeping D03 high is a bet on option value, not on present proof
cruxes.would_change_if: Compute-normalized, pre-registered experiments appear that show sustained multi-round gains in real capability, not cherry-picked results

taste_advice: Do not use valuation or narrative to decide whether to do research: capital price and research opportunity are two clocks and can be read separately; what you should really look at is who the returns land with and how long they last

pairwise.why: Without credible evaluation there is no way to know whether the world model's contribution is real
Claims about robot reliability likewise need evaluation to be believed
Separation-protocol-style research has a low capital barrier and is still open; the reliability bottleneck of embodied AI leans more toward engineering iteration
The world model is more fundamental; the policy head is only one implementation of it and is more replaceable
Simulation directly addresses the hard bottleneck of scarce real data and is closer to the root cause than embodied AI as a whole
D03 still bets on the scarce learning-by-doing mechanism, but, given how much I underrated D02's reliability value, the two are closer than they look
The gap in understanding tasks has not been closed; generation is already being commoditized and caught in price wars
The pre-training door is already closed to academia; evaluation is one of the few positions that combine a low barrier with a real bottleneck
Scaffolding is being absorbed by models; the core problem of continual learning is unsolved, so the moat is deeper
The value of safety and alignment is realized through regulation, an external variable; evaluation is an internal bottleneck that cannot be bypassed
The shake-out in autonomous driving has begun and requires fleet access; the shake-out in embodied AI has not fully arrived

changes.argument_restated: The economic value of reliable deployed execution is underestimated, even if it does not count as teaching a new reasoning paradigm
changes.why: Gains in efficiency and reliability have real ROIC value, which is consistent with how I view D14 systems efficiency; my earlier score for it was too low

changes.argument_restated: Going heavy refers to research time, not capital; the two should be assessed separately
changes.why: C5 and C6 independently converged on the same distinction, which shows the research opportunity itself is higher than the window score I originally gave

held_despite.why: METR's 70-90% compute trial-and-error, the withdrawn DGM cost figure and others all confirm the evidence is thin, but D03 is a bet on option value, not on present proof

still_disagree: X3: the evidence gap at the decision-driving layer and the inflated valuations exist together, and the fact that research timing is early does not prove the price is reasonable; X5: validation progress is not structural importance, and I still bet that D08 is harder to replicate
learned: Capital price and research timing are two clocks that can be read separately; C5/C6 independently converged on the same distinction in overtime, which led me to score D08's window and the research opportunity itself separately
